title: Do Verifiers Reduce Security-Relevant Misconfigurations? A Preregistered Paired Evaluation of Verifier-in-the-Loop GVR for Intent-to-Configuration
abstract: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired experiment to test whether embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a generate–verify–repair (GVR) loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline. Under a frozen adapter contract that used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one LLM candidate replayed to both arms), N = 300 matched intents (150 benign + 150 adversarial variants) were evaluated in a Dockerized FRRouting-style emulation with two deterministic validators combined by logical OR. The run completed planned episodes = 600, model_calls_used = 300, and failed episodes = 0. Primary outcome: baseline_success = 300 and guarded_success = 300 (paired contingency n11 = 300; n10 = n01 = n00 = 0). Paired risk-difference = 0.0, exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.0, 95% bootstrap CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729) = [0.0, 0.0]. Observing 0/300 violations yields a one-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound ≈ 0.00994 on an undetected baseline violation rate. Crucially, the repair step was never invoked because validators never flagged forbidden reachability; therefore the study quantifies that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline already satisfies the safety predicate under the chosen contract, but it does not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations. We succinctly define the scoring predicate and validator assumptions, report the compact confirmatory statistics, and point to the archived preregistration and deterministic execution artifacts to support reproducibility and targeted follow-up stress tests.

sections.introduction:
Motivation and research question. Large language models (LLMs) are now used to translate high-level operator intent into device configurations. Operator concerns focus on security-relevant regression: generated configurations that expand attack surface or violate access-control invariants. Prior system and survey work therefore recommends constrained generation, execution oracles, and iterative generate–verify–repair (GVR) loops as mitigations [1,2,3]. However, rigorous confirmatory evidence that placing a formal verifier inside a GVR loop reduces security-increasing (forbidden-reachability) misconfigurations under adversarial intents is limited.

Research question and contributions. We asked: Does embedding a reachability/policy verifier inside a GVR loop reduce the incidence of forbidden-reachability misconfigurations produced by an LLM-driven intent→configuration pipeline? To answer this we preregistered and executed a paired N = 300 confirmatory design (cnd-2026-netops-gvr-security-01-prereg-v1). Our contributions are: (1) a preregistered, deterministic paired experiment comparing single-pass LLM generation (baseline) to an LLM+verifier GVR pipeline (guarded) under a shared_initial_candidate contract; (2) a compact, artifact-grounded statistical report showing a degenerate confirmatory outcome (n11 = 300) together with exact-test and bootstrap inference and a Clopper–Pearson upper-bound on undetected violation rate; (3) a concise technical definition of the forbidden-reachability predicate and each validator's detection assumptions; and (4) operational design lessons and reproducibility pointers to guide follow-up stress tests that intentionally exercise the repair path.
sections.related_work: Prior experimental and systems work motivates our approach but leaves open the specific verifier-in-the-loop security question. Generate–verify–repair and execution-guided repair architectures have improved correctness for code and infrastructure tasks; verifier strength and repair policy influence realized gains (e.g., TerraFormer et al. [1]). Surveys and NetOps system papers document LLM failure modes (hallucination, overconfidence, domain mismatch) and consistently recommend validators or constrained generation [2,4]. Emulation/testbed research demonstrates that execution-based validation is feasible for research evaluation but cautions about external-validity gaps relative to production devices [3]. Unlike prior work, our study applies a preregistered paired confirmatory design with deterministic validators and archived per-episode traces to obtain audit-ready, reproducible accounting relevant to whether verifier insertion reduces observed forbidden-reachability errors under the chosen contract.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and design. The preregistration fixed a paired binary design with N = 300 matched intents (150 benign seeds and 150 programmatic adversarial variants), primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, and an exact McNemar two-sided confirmatory test (alpha = 0.05). Sampling, deduplication (exact and fuzzy edit-distance rules), exclusion rules, repair budget (≤1 repair call per triggered pair), and missingness handling were prespecified. The preregistration and the execution manifest are archived in the evidence bundle for verification.

Adapter contract and generation semantics. To conserve provider budget the executed adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics: one initial LLM candidate per matched intent was generated and replayed identically to both arms (baseline is a replay, guarded first validates and may invoke at most one repair call if a validator detects forbidden reachability). This contract yields one hosted-model generation per pair (model_calls_used = 300) instead of two independent draws per pair; the shared contract reduces provider usage but also reduces independent-sample variability needed to observe discordant violations between arms.

Predicate and validators (concise technical definition). Forbidden-reachability predicate: for a given task the predicate reports true if any validator observes a forwarding path that violates the task-specified protection semantics for that scenario (the task payloads declare protected interfaces and workflow policies; violations reflect configurations that enable reachability disallowed by those policies). Execution validator (Batfish-style): performs concrete packet-forwarding simulation on the emulated topology including ACL and route-policy semantics as modeled by the emulator; it reports predicate violations when a simulated forwarding path reaches a protected interface that the task forbids. Static reachability analyzer: constructs a device–interface reachability graph from declared configuration statements and performs deterministic graph reachability checks (it abstracts dynamic route convergence and may therefore miss transient route-policy effects). Validators were combined with a logical-OR rule: a pair is labeled violating if any validator reports forbidden reachability. Known limitations: the execution validator depends on the fidelity of emulator-implemented ACL/route-policy semantics; the static analyzer is conservative with respect to dynamic behaviors and may produce false negatives for transient route-policy violations. These definitions and per-episode validator outputs are archived in the scoring artifacts for audit.
sections.results:
Execution accounting. Planned episodes = 600 (300 pairs × 2 arms); completed = 600; failed = 0; model_calls_used = 300 under shared_initial_candidate semantics. Provider-call auditing recorded stage 'shared_initial_generation' = 300. Representative verification artifacts and their hashes (three representative items are provided to permit spot-checking of archive integrity): execution/model_configuration.json (sha256: a40e96e212ab87da...), execution/raw_results.jsonl (sha256: 36ea4a5dfa90384f...), execution/task_manifest.jsonl (sha256: 62bd1fe90a9ad7b2...). Primary confirmatory statistics (compact). Table 1 displays the paired contingency and principal inferential numbers.

Table 1 (compact): Paired primary outcome
- n11 (both pass): 300
- n10 (guarded pass only): 0
- n01 (baseline pass only): 0
- n00 (both fail): 0
- Paired risk-difference (guarded − baseline): 0.0
- Exact McNemar two-sided p-value: 1.0
- 95% bootstrap percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed 1729): [0.0, 0.0]
- One-sided Clopper–Pearson 95% upper bound on baseline violation rate: ≈0.00994

Repair activity and verifier concordance. Validators never reported forbidden reachability on any initial candidate; therefore no repair call was issued for any pair (repair_applied=false in every per-episode trace). Verifier disagreement rate across the two validators was 0 for this run. Because no discordant pairs occurred (n10 = n01 = 0) the McNemar paired test is uninformative about repair efficacy: there were no initial-candidate violations that repair could have corrected under the executed contract.

Representative examples. Representative per-task normalized configurations and validator_trace summaries are archived for manual inspection; one typical medium-difficulty example follows the shutdown_configure_restore pattern and both validators reported valid final states with violation_count = 0.
sections.discussion:
Interpretation and what the evidence supports. Under the specific contract and experimental elements used here (shared_initial_candidate; declared model gpt-5-mini; two deterministic validators combined by OR; the supplied task set and emulator), baseline generation already satisfied the forbidden-reachability predicate for all sampled intents; hence verifier insertion did not change observed compliance. The archived artifacts consistently support this statement (provider accounting, per-episode validator traces, and the paired contingency are mutually consistent).

What the evidence does not show. Because the repair path was never invoked, the experiment provides no evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue violating initial candidates. The preregistered power calculation assumed a nonzero baseline violation rate and targeted a 30 percentage-point absolute reduction; the degenerate observed contingency violates that assumption and renders the confirmatory McNemar test moot for repair efficacy.

Design lessons and operational implications. (1) Generation semantics matter: shared_initial_candidate reduces model calls but also reduces independent-sample variance that can produce repair-exercising discordances; independent-condition generation (two draws per pair) or larger N/model-call budgets should be used to evaluate repair efficacy. (2) Adversary potency matters: programmatic adversarial variants used here did not trigger validator-detectable forbidden reachability; stronger or targeted adversaries are needed to exercise repair. (3) Verifier strength matters: diverse, higher-fidelity oracles and richer dynamic simulation increase the chance of detecting true violations. (4) Reproducibility is practical: per-episode raw responses, validator traces, and provider-call audits are archived to permit exact replay and targeted stress tests.
sections.conclusion: We preregistered and executed a deterministic paired evaluation of a verifier-in-the-loop GVR pipeline for intent→configuration generation. The run completed N = 300 paired intents with model_calls_used = 300 under shared_initial_candidate semantics and produced a degenerate outcome: baseline and guarded arms both passed the forbidden-reachability predicate on all pairs (n11 = 300). Because validators never detected violations, no repair was invoked; therefore the experiment quantifies that inserting a verifier does not change observed compliance when baseline is already compliant under the chosen contract, but it does not provide evidence that verifier-guided repair can rescue genuine violations. Follow-up experiments that (a) use independent-condition generation, (b) increase repair-call budgets, (c) employ stronger targeted adversaries, and (d) broaden verifier diversity are required to test repair efficacy. We release the preregistration and deterministic execution artifacts to support reproducible stress tests and targeted follow-up work.

limitations: Degenerate confirmatory outcome: zero discordant pairs (n11 = 300, n10 = n01 = n00 = 0) render the paired McNemar test uninformative about repair efficacy because no initial-candidate violations were observed.

GVR repair path not exercised: validators never detected forbidden reachability for the sampled intents, so the experiment tests whether verifier insertion changes compliance when baseline is already compliant, not whether verifier-guided repair rescues violations.

Generation contract choice: shared_initial_candidate produced one LLM call per pair (model_calls_used = 300) and limited independent draws that could produce repair-exercising discordances; independent-condition generation or larger model-call budgets are recommended for repair-focused tests.

Adversarial potency and external validity: programmatic adversarial variants used here did not trigger validator-detectable violations; tasks were synthetic and executed in deterministic emulator images and may not generalize to heterogeneous production devices or live traffic.
Model and verifier scope: single declared model (gpt-5-mini) and two deterministic validators were evaluated; results may differ with other LLMs, stronger oracles, or richer dynamic simulation.
